rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zīna may be accusative of purpose, circumstantial if jaʿalnā means ‘created,’ or a second object if it means ‘made’; li-hā may express purpose with zīna, be an extra lām, or modify an omitted adjective of zīna.
rows.anchor: أن ينتصب على المفعول له، وأن يتنصب على الحال إن جعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Linabluwهم is attached to jaʿalnā under either of its meanings, ‘created’ or ‘made.’
rows.anchor: " لنبلوهم " متعلق ب " جعلنا " بمعنييه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyuhum may be interrogative: a subject with aḥsanu as predicate, its clause occupying the object position of linabluwهم because testing is a cause of knowing, like asking or looking.
rows.anchor: يجوز في " أيهم " وجهان، أحدهما: أن تكون استفهامية مرفوعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ayyuhum is a relative pronoun meaning ‘the one who’; aḥsanu predicates an omitted subject, and the clause is its relative clause, with the pronoun substituting for the object of linabluwهم.
rows.anchor: أنها موصولة بمعنى الذي " وأحسن " خبر مبتدأ مضمر، والجملة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: On the relative analysis, the nominative ending of ayyuhum can be indeclinable: it is formally annexed and the start of its relative clause is omitted, meeting the conditions for building it.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب سيبويه، وأن تكون للإعراب لأن البناء جائز لا واجب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative may instead be inflectional because building is permissible, not obligatory; an anomalous Maryam reading has inflected ayyuhum.
rows.anchor: ومن الإعراب ما قرئ به شاذا أيهم أشد على الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verse about greeting whichever of the Banu Mālik is best supplies poetic usage for ayyuhum with a nominative ending.
rows.anchor: فسلم على أيهم أفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns in linabluwهم and ayyuhum refer to the earth’s inhabitants inferred from context; another analysis refers to what is on earth if it means rational beings. Exegetes identify them as shepherds, or scholars, righteous people, and caliphs.
rows.anchor: والضمير في " لنبلوهم " و " أيهم " عائد على ما يفهم من السياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿīdan is the second object because jaʿalnā here can only mean transformation or making something into something else.
rows.anchor: مفعول ثان، لأن الجعل هنا تصيير ليس إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿīd means soil, and juruz describes land without vegetation; a dry year has no rain and barren land has no plants.
rows.anchor: والصعيد. التراب: والجرز: الذي لا نبات به. يقال: سنة جزر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarazat describes vegetation disappearing through drought or locusts; jaraza al-arḍ al-jarādu means locusts ate everything in it. Jarrūz can mean a gluttonous woman, as the cited comic line illustrates.
rows.anchor: وجرزت الأرض: إذا ذهب نباتها بقحط أو جراد وجرز الأرض الجراد: أكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Am is discontinuous, estimated as bal for transition plus an interrogative hamza by most grammarians; others estimate bal alone or the hamza alone.
rows.anchor: هذه منقطعة فتقدر ب " بل " التي للانتقال لا للإبطال، وبهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause beginning in may supply both objects of ḥasiba or just one, according to the familiar grammatical disagreement.
rows.anchor: " ان " وما في حيزها سادة [مسد] المفعولين أو أحدهما على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kahf means any cave according to one view, or specifically a spacious opening in a mountain; a narrower opening is a ghār. Its common plural is kuhūf and its less common plural akhuf.
rows.anchor: قيل: مطلق الغار. وقيل: هو ما اتسع في الجبل، فإن لم يتسع فهو غار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raqīm has been explained as ‘inscribed,’ ‘one who inscribes,’ or the name of the Companions’ dog; Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s verse is cited using al-raqīm.
rows.anchor: والرقيم: قيل: بمعنى مرقوم. وقيل: بمعنى راقم. وقيل: هو اسم

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Umayya’s verse says al-raqīm is beside the hunt while the people sleep in the cave, illustrating Arabic use of the word.
rows.anchor: وأنشدوا لأمية بن أبي الصلت: 3125- وليس بها إلا الرقيم مجاورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAjaban may be the predicate with min āyātinā circumstantial, a second predicate with min āyātinā first, or a circumstantial accusative from the implicit pronoun in min āyātinā. Its singular form reflects its origin as a verbal noun; alternatively it modifies an omitted āya or stands for āya dhāt ʿajab by ellipsis.
rows.anchor: " عجبا " يجوز أن تكون خبرا، و { من آياتنا } حال منه، وأن يكون خبرا ثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qawmunā may be apposition or clarification of hāʾulāʾi, with ittakhadhū as predicate; alternatively qawmunā is predicate and ittakhadhū circumstantial. Ittakhadha takes one object meaning ‘made/carved’ or two meaning ‘made into,’ with min dūnihi as the second object placed first.
rows.anchor: يجوز في " قومنا " أن يكون بدلا أو بيانا، و " اتخذوا " هو خبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the one-object analysis, min dūnihi can attach to ittakhadhū or be an omitted circumstantial modifier of ālihatan, which could otherwise take it as an adjective if it followed.
rows.anchor: وعلى الوجه الأول يجوز في " من دونه " أن يتعلق ب " اتخذوا "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lawlā yāʾtūna is an exhortation carrying denial; ʿalayhim means ‘about their worship’ or ‘about their taking them as gods,’ with the understood noun omitted.
rows.anchor: لولا يأتون } تخصيص فيه معنى الإنكار. و " عليهم " ، أي: على عبادتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request clause cannot be an adjective of ālihatan because a demand clause is incompatible with that syntax and meaning.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن تكون هذه الجملة التخضيضية صفة ل " آلهة " لفساده معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Estimating an omitted ‘they said’ after the cited line about bringing a mixture and asking whether one has seen a wolf does not rescue the adjective analysis, because it makes the meaning defective.
rows.anchor: جاؤوا بمذق هل رأيت الذئب قط لم يساعدك المعنى لفساده عليه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in innahum may refer to aḥad, singular in form but collective in meaning; al-Zamakhsharī instead takes it as ahl appended to the town pronoun, or it may refer to their people inferred from context.
rows.anchor: هذا الضمير يجوز أن يعود على " أحد " لأنه في معنى الجمع، وأن يكون

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads yaẓharū as passive, ‘if you are discovered/overpowered by them’; idhan is a conditional answer and consequence: if they appear over you, you will not succeed.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي " يظهروا " مبنيا للمفعول و " إذن " جواب وجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation supplies an omitted transition: after answering the question about the cave, the Prophet is told to ask their number, so sīn marks the prediction; following coordinated verbs inherit its future force.
rows.anchor: قيل: إنما أتي بالسين في هذا لأن في الكلام طيا وإدماجا

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin assimilates emphatic thāʾ into feminine tāʾ because their articulations are close, both are voiceless, and they follow a quiescent weak letter.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن " ثلاث " بإدغام الثاء المثلثة في تاء التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause rābiʿuhum kalbuhum is nominative as an adjective modifying thalātha.
rows.anchor: الجملة في محل رفع صفة ل " ثلاثة ".

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: In one narration Ibn Kathīr reads khamsata with fatḥa on the mīm, an idiom also found in ʿashara.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير في رواية بفتح الميم، وهي لغة كعشرة.

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin is reported to read khamsa with kasra on khāʾ and mīm and assimilate its tāʾ into the sīn of sādisihim; the author calls this very heavy and suspects an error in the attribution. Another report has tanwīn assimilated into sīn without nasalization.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن بكسر الخاء والميم، وبإدغام التاء في السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thalātha, khamsa, and sabʿa predicate an omitted subject (‘they are three/five/seven’); the following clauses modify three and five, not ungoverned circumstantial clauses or demonstrative estimates, since no present group was indicated.
rows.anchor: و " ثلاثة " و " خمسة " و " سبعة " إخبار لمبتدأ مضمر، أي: هم ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajman bil-ghayb has four parses: accusative of purpose, circumstantial ‘guessing,’ governed by yaqūlūn because it conveys that meaning, or governed by an implied cognate verb (‘they conjecture a conjecture’). Rajm originally means throwing small stones and came to mean conjecture.
rows.anchor: قوله: { رجما بالغيب } فيه أربعة أوجه، أحدها: أنه مفعول من أجله؛

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s verse says war is not something merely conjectured or hearsay, witnessing murajjam in the sense ‘conjectured.’
rows.anchor: قال زهير: 3139- وما الحرب إلا ما علمتم وذقتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account makes the wāw coordinate with ‘they are seven,’ recording two assertions by the disputants; another treats it as a new divine statement. Al-Zamakhsharī calls it an adjective-introducing emphatic wāw, which the Sheikh rejects because grammarians do not recognize it.
rows.anchor: أنها عاطفة، عطفت هذه الجملة على جملة قوله " هم سبعة "

rows.speaker: ابن خالويه
rows.claim: Ibn Khālawayh and Abū Bakr, transmitter of ʿĀṣim, call it the ‘wāw of eight’: Quraysh allegedly inserted wāw when counting from seven to eight. Some applied this to Paradise’s eight gates versus Hell’s seven in 39:73.
rows.anchor: ذكر ذلك ابن خالويه وأبو بكر راوي عاصم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading k-albihim means ‘owner of their dog’; some therefore supply ṣāḥib in the ordinary reading too.
rows.anchor: وقرئ: " كالبهم " ، أي: صاحب كلبهم.

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Sheikh supplies ‘persons’ as the omitted counted noun because rābiʿuhum means the dog makes them four; ‘men’ would mix incompatible counted kinds. The author praises this as sound.
rows.anchor: فقدره الشيخ: ثلاثة أشخاص، قال: " وإنما قدرنا أشخاصا لأن رابعهم

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ says rābiʿuhum cannot function as an active participle governing an understood object because it describes a past event.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: " ولا يعمل اسم الفاعل هنا لأنه ماض ".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author replies that it means the dog makes the group four and so governs implicitly; it works in the past by depicting the situation as present, like bāsiṭ.
rows.anchor: وليس كما زعم فإن المعنى على: يصير الكلب لهم أربعة، فهو ناصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The specified object of biʾsa al-sharāb is omitted and estimated as ‘that is,’ namely the water they seek for relief.
rows.anchor: المخصوص محذوف تقديره: هو، أي: ذلك الماء المستغاث به.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāʾat is a regular inflected verb with Hell as subject; murtafaqan is transferred from subject to specification, meaning its resting place is evil. Murtafaq can mean a place to recline, a dwelling, or the verbal noun of comfort.
rows.anchor: " ساءت " هنا متصرفة على بابها. وفاعلها ضمير النار. ومرتفقا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The contrast with ‘how good a resting place’ in 18:31 is rhetorical pairing, since Hell affords no comfort; al-Zamakhsharī suggests sarcasm, citing Imruʾ al-Qays’s line about reclining through the night.
rows.anchor: وهو من باب المقابلة أيضا كقوله في وصف الجنة بعد: وحسنت مرتفقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inna lā nuḍīʿ may predicate inna alladhīna; possible links are repetition of the expressed noun by meaning, as al-Akhfash permits even in relative clauses, an omitted minhum, or generic reference.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون خبر { إن الذين } والرابط: إما تكرر الظاهر بمعناه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ulāʾika lahum jannāt is the predicate and inna lā nuḍīʿ parenthetical; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives a similar poetic example, though the Sheikh says that example could instead be a predicate. The author clarifies Ibn ʿAṭiyya offered only one possible analysis; both clauses may also be predicates where multiple predicates are allowed.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الخبر قوله: { أولئك لهم جنات } ، ويكون قوله: { إنا لا نضيع } اعتراضا.

rows.speaker: الثقفي
rows.claim: Al-Thaqafī reads lā nuḍayyiʿ with a doubled consonant, making it transitive by gemination as the majority do with hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الثقفي " لا نضيع " بالتشديد، عداه بالتشديد كما عداه الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in min asāwir can mark origin, partitive meaning, genus explanation (‘some bracelets’), or be redundant according to al-Akhfash, supported by 76:21; Abū al-Baqāʾ lists the three latter analyses.
rows.anchor: في " من " هذه أربعة أوجه، أحدها: أنها للابتداء. والثاني: أنها للتعيض.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asāwir is plural of aswira, itself plural of siwār: a plural of a plural from iswār; Abū ʿUbayda instead says the plural drops the augment from iswār, whose original form is asāwīr. A cited poem uses iswār.
rows.anchor: وأساور جمع أسورة، وأسورة جمع سوار، كحمار وأحمرة، فهو جمع الجمع.

rows.speaker: أبان بن عاصم
rows.claim: Abān ibn ʿĀṣim reads aswira as a plural of siwār; the author says these readings will be discussed among the canonical readings in al-Zukhruf.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان بن عاصم " أسورة " جمع سوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Siwār has the small plural aswira and large plural sūr with still wāw, patterned like qadhil/humur; the wāw is still because it is weak, though a poem vocalizes it for metrical necessity. Lexicographers define siwār as arm jewelry of gold, silver, or copper, while ivory jewelry is qalb.
rows.anchor: والسوار يجمع في القلة على " أسورة " وفي الكثرة على " سور " بسكون الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min dhahab may explain the material or be partitive; it may modify an omitted adjective of asāwir in the genitive or attach to yuḥallawna in the accusative. Wa-yalbasūna coordinates with yuḥallawna; passive adornment signals that others do it for them, while a person dresses himself, and adornment precedes clothing because it is more desired.
rows.anchor: من ذهب } يجوز أن تكون للبيان، وأن تكون للتبعيض. ويجوز أن تتعلق بمحذوف

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s line about girls adorned with jewels witnesses the passive sense that another person adorns them.
rows.anchor: كقول امرئ القيس. 3155- غرائر في كن وصون ونعمة يحلين ياقوتا

rows.speaker: أبان بن عاصم
rows.claim: Abān ibn ʿĀṣim reads yalbisūna with kasra on the bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان بن عاصم " ويلبسون " بكسر الباء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in min sundusin wa-istabraq explains the kind of garments. Sundus is fine brocade and istabraq coarse; whether these are plurals is disputed, as is whether istabraq is Arabic from brilliance or a Persian loan; it is also called silk, and Ibn Baḥr says gold-woven fabric. Sundus is fuʿlul with root nūn.
rows.anchor: قوله: { من سندس وإستبرق } " من " لبيان الجنس وهي نعت لثياب.

rows.speaker: المرقش
rows.claim: Al-Muraqqish’s verse pairs istabraq with dibāj clothing, fitting the garment and brocade glosses.
rows.anchor: وأنشد للمرقش: 3156- تراهن يلبسن المشاعر مرة وإستبرق الديباج

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads wa-stabraq with connecting hamza, fatḥa on qāf, and no tanwīn; Ibn Jinnī calls it an oversight. The author rejects indeclinability because it is a common noun, while another analysis makes it a past verb from brilliance.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن " واستبرق " بوصل الهمزة وفتح القاف غير منونة.

rows.speaker: الأهوازي
rows.claim: Al-Ahwāzī’s al-Iqnāʿ reports the connected form with fatḥa on qāf and no declension; the author sees no basis to indecline it. The author of al-Lawāmiʿ records only hamza connection and keeps it declinable, allowing irregular hamza deletion or Arabic derivation; the author favors Arabic origin and inflection.
rows.anchor: وقال الأهوازي في " الإقناع ": " واستبرق بالوصل وفتح/ القاف حيث كان لا يصرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muttaʾkiʾīn is circumstantial; arāʾik is plural arīka, a bed only under a canopy, though another view includes couches within canopies too. Al-Rāghib explains arīka as a canopy over a bed, perhaps from arāk wood or from residence, originally staying to graze arāk and later generalized.
rows.anchor: " متكئين " حال والأرائك: جمع أريكة وهي الأسرة بشرط أن تكون في الحجال

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads ʿalā al-arāʾik as ʿal-arāʾik by transferring the hamza vowel to the article’s lām and assimilating the two lām sounds after the alif drops. A poetic spelling ʿal-arḍ witnesses the same sound change; an analogous al-Baqara reading is bimā unzaylik.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن: " علرائك " وذلك: أنه نقل حركة الهمزة إلى لام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ḍaraba mathalan, ḍaraba may take two objects, as discussed in al-Baqara; Abū al-Baqāʾ parses an omitted mathal mithla rajulayni, with jaʿalnā explaining mathal, or takes it as an accusative adjective of rajulayni.
rows.anchor: قد تقدم أن " ضرب " مع المثل، يجوز أن يتعدى لاثنين في سورة البقرة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaffa bi-shayʾ means to surround it on every side; the Nābigha’s line uses it for encircling. Ḥaffa people means they made a ring around it, and ḥaffaftuhu bihi means I made it surrounded by it.
rows.anchor: وحففناهما } يقال: حف بالشيء: طاف به من جميع جوانبه، قال النابغة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kiltā is the subject and ātat its predicate; the verse follows common agreement with its grammatical feminine form rather than the dual meaning.
rows.anchor: قد تقدم في السورة قبلها حكم " كلتا " وهي مبتدأ، و " آتت " خبرها.

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads masculine kilā because feminine gender is figurative, then feminine ātat to agree with jannatayn, like ‘the sun rose and shone’; al-Farrāʾ transmits another reading kull al-jannatayn ātā aklahu, resuming agreement with kull.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله - وكذلك هي في مصحفه - " كلا الجنتين " بالتذكير

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: The common fajjarnā is geminated for intensification though there is one river; Yaʿqūb and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read the lighter form, also reported from al-Aʿmash in al-Qamar, where gemination better fits ‘springs.’
rows.anchor: العامة على التشديد وإنما كان كذلك، وهو نهر واحد مبالغة فيه.

rows.speaker: أبو السمال والفياض
rows.claim: The ordinary reading has an open hāʾ in nahr; Abū al-Sammāl and al-Fayyāḍ have it quiescent.
rows.anchor: والعامة على فتح هاء " نهر " وأبو السمال والفياض بسكونها.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Thamar with ḍamma means wealth; Ibn ʿAbbās says it includes gold, silver, livestock, and all other property, while another view restricts it to gold and silver. The Nābigha’s line witnesses athmara for wealth and children; Abū Rajāʾ reads bi-thamarihi with fatḥa and a quiescent mīm.
rows.anchor: وتقدم أن " الثمر " بالضم المال. فقال ابن عباس: جميع المال من ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-huwa yuḥāwiruhu is a circumstantial clause clarifying dialogue, since mere speech does not entail conversation; muḥāwara is reciprocal speech from ḥāra, ‘returned,’ as in 84:14 and Imruʾ al-Qays’s verse about a meteor turning to ash. It may describe subject or object.
rows.anchor: " وهو يحاوره " جملة حالية مبينة إذ لا يلزم من القول المحاورة؛

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ explains the singular ‘his garden’ after two gardens as using one for the pair, citing a Hudhalī line with singular feminine agreement after ḥidāq; the author corrects that the pronouns refer to the broken plural, not one ḥadaqa.
rows.anchor: إنما أفرد بعد ذكر التثنية اكتفاء بالواحد للعلم بالحال. قال أبو البقاء:

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says ‘he entered what is his garden’: he owns no other garden, has no share in the promised Garden, and treats worldly property as his sole garden, without intending the dual or either garden specifically. The Sheikh objects; the author replies he need not mean simultaneous entry into both but means the wording does not designate one or two. Abū al-Baqāʾ says both belong to him and so count as one thing.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " فإن قلت: لم أفرد الجنة بعد التثنية؟ قلت: معناه: ودخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-huwa ẓālim is circumstantial of dakhala’s subject; li-nafsihi is object of ẓālim, with extra lām because the governing word is derived. Qāla lahu ṣāḥibuhu may be circumstantial or a new clause explaining the injustice; the author prefers the latter.
rows.anchor: قوله: " وهو ظالم " حال من فاعل " دخل " ، و " لنفسه "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabīda means ‘perish’; bāda yabīdu has the verbal nouns biyūdan and baydūdatan, the latter like kaynūna after one yāʾ is deleted, on the pattern fayʿalūla.
rows.anchor: " أن تبيد " ، أي: تهلك، قال: 3162- فلئن باد أهله

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and the Kufans read minha in the singular, following the nearest mention, jannatahu; Iraqi codices omit the mīm.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو والكوفيون " منها " بالإفراد نظرا إلى أقرب مذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readers have minhumā in the dual, following the two gardens and kiltā al-jannatayn; Meccan, Medinan, and Syrian codices include the mīm, and each reading matches its codex.
rows.anchor: والباقون " منهما " بالتثنية نظرا إلى الأصل في قوله: " جنتين "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuṭfa originally means a drop of clear water, from naṭafa ‘to drip’; a hadith says ‘his head dripped,’ with a variant ‘it poured’ explaining it, and semen is called a drop by analogy.
rows.anchor: النطفة في الأصل: القطرة من الماء الصافي يقال: نطف ينطف، أي: قطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajulan may be circumstantial despite being neither derived nor transient, since it follows sawāka and God could have made him other than a man; the giraffe example and a poetic comparison support this. Alternatively, it is a second object of sawāka, implying ṣayyaraka or jaʿalaka, as al-Ḥawfī holds.
rows.anchor: " رجلا " فيه وجهان، أحدهما: أنه حال، وجاز ذلك وإن [كان] غير منتقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir retains the alif in connection and at pause; others omit it in connection and retain it at pause, so all agree at pause. The word derives from lakin anā by moving hamza’s vowel, deleting hamza, and assimilating the nūns, which the author prefers over arbitrary hamza deletion. Ordinary readers follow the rule for connected anā; Nāfiʿ usually retains its alif before hamza, while Ibn ʿĀmir follows the written form, also a Tamīmī dialect.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر بإثبات الألف وصلا ووقفا، والباقون بحذفها وصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible syntax: anā, huwa, and Allāh as nested subjects with rabbī the third predicate and yāʾ as linker; Allāh may instead clarify huwa if it refers to the creator. Other parses make huwa the subject, an emphasis, or a separator; it cannot be a pronoun of the matter under one analysis because the predicate clause lacks a linker to lakin’s subject.
rows.anchor: وإعراب ذلك: أن يكون " أنا " مبتدأ و " هو " مبتدأ ثان، و " هو " ضمير الشأن

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr reads lakinnah at pause with hāʾ al-sakt to show the nūn vowel; the author cites Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī’s line as another example.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو " لكنه " بهاء السكت وقفا؛ لأن القصد بيان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports through Hārūn a reading from Abū ʿAmr, lakinnahu huwa Allāh, with a pronoun attached to lakin; the author infers the hāʾ is not hāʾ al-sakt.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية عن أبي عمرو: " روى عنه هارون " لكنه هو الله

rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī unusually parses lakinnā as lakin plus nā, from lakinnan after deleting one nūn; the construction should have been rabbunā and ‘we do not associate with our Lord,’ but the speaker considered the meaning and used singular. The author calls this very odd; ordinary lakin cannot be operative with a nominative pronoun after it.
rows.anchor: وخرجه الفارسي على وجه غريب: وهو أن تكون " لكنا " لكن واسمها

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads lakin anā huwa without transfer or assimilation; Ibn Khālawayh reports from him lakin huwa Allāh without anā, and another reading is lakinnanā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله " لكن أنا هو " على الأصل من غير نقل ولا إدغام.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the connected alif as compensation for deleted hamza and cites poetry deriving lakin iyyāka from lakin anā by vowel transfer, deletion, and assimilation. The Sheikh says the name of lakin may instead be omitted, as in another poem; the author says al-Zamakhsharī did not claim his reading was exclusive.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وحسن ذلك -يعني إثبات الأف في الوصل- وقوع الألف عوضا

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: Basran grammarians explain a poetic lām apparently entering the predicate of lakin as underlying lakin innī: transfer and deletion leave the lām in the predicate of inna; the author notes some call the verse fabricated and its poet unknown.
rows.anchor: وخرجه البصريون على أن الأصل: ولكن إني من حبها، ثم نقل حركة همزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lākinnā corrects the accusation ‘Have you disbelieved?’ as if saying ‘You are a disbeliever, but I am a believer’; the question demands acknowledgment, like ‘Zayd is absent but ʿAmr is present,’ since one might assume both are absent.
rows.anchor: والاستدراك من قوله " أكفرت " ، كأنه قال لأخيه: أنت كافر؛ لأنه استفهام تقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥusbānan is a verbal noun of ḥasaba, ‘to count.’ Al-Zajjāj calls it a calculated punishment accounting for what one’s hands earned, which the author approves. Al-Rāghib says it is what is accounted and requited; Abū Isḥāq and al-Zamakhsharī agree, the latter calling it a divinely measured judgment to destroy the garden.
rows.anchor: الحسبان/ مصدر حسب الشيء يحسبه، أي: أحصاه. قال الزجاج: " أي عذاب حسبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes ḥusbān as plural of ḥusbāna, an arrow; tafsir also describes it as pieces of fire or as lightning bolts.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو جمع حسبانة وهي السهم. وفي التفسير: أنها قطع من نار.

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: Aw yaṣbiḥ is coordinated with yursil; the Sheikh notes sinking water does not result from a heavenly calamity unless ḥusbān means divine decree, which could make either the garden a slippery plain or its water sink.
rows.anchor: " أو يصبح " عطف على قوله: " ويرسل " لأن غؤور الماء لا يتسبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zalaq and ghawr are verbal nouns used as emphatic adjectives; ghāra al-māʾ means water receded and went into the earth. Most read fatḥa on ghayn, al-Barjamī uses ḍamma, and a group reads ghūran with ḍamma on ghayn and hamza, also a verbal noun like julūsan.
rows.anchor: والزلق والغور في الأصل: مصدران وصف بهما مبالغة. والعامة على فتح الغين.

rows.speaker: الأخوان
rows.claim: The two readers read yakun with yāʾ; the rest read takun with tāʾ. Both are acceptable because feminine gender is figurative and the intervening phrase favors masculine agreement.
rows.anchor: قرأ الأخوان " يكن " بالياء من تحت. والباقون من فوق، وهما واضحتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yansurūnahu may be the predicate, apparently; alternatively it is circumstantial with the preceding prepositional phrase as predicate, permitted from an indefinite after negation, or an adjective of fiʾa if the prepositional phrase is predicate. Its masculine plural matches the collective meaning ‘people,’ while feminine-form agreement is singular as in 3:13; Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads tanṣuruhu, and the author confirms it is attested.
rows.anchor: " ينصرونه " يجوز أن تكون هذه الجملة خبرا وهو الظاهر، وأن تكون حالية
